└────────► Better compiler optimizations
—> A miniature end-to-end AI compiler and optimization
framework that can take a neural network or compute kernel,
optimize it through multiple compiler stages, execute it,
measure its performance, and automatically search for better
execution strategies.
—> This project is not tied to one language or one processor, but it
is specialized for AI and tensor-computation workloads. It builds a
portable compiler pipeline that can optimize those workloads and, with
appropriate backends, generate code for different hardware targets
instead of being locked to a single device.
What is IREE?
IREE is an MLIR-based compiler and runtime system.
The compiler turns machine learning models into optimized
executable modules, and the runtime loads those modules,
feeds them input tensors, executes them on the
target device, and returns the results.

Brief 4
Take a small PyTorch model → lower it to IREE-runnable
form (.mlir → .vmfb, using existing tooling) → write/generate
the minimal C/C++ host code that uses IREE's high-level
runtime API (not low-level HAL buffers/semaphores) to load, invoke,
and read results → validate it against a provided mock/stub
runtime, and against the real PyTorch output for numerical correctness.
No custom hardware, no hand-written low-level dispatch.

Whole Project
The IREE compiler generates FlatBuffer files using the .vmfb file extension,
short for "Virtual Machine FlatBuffer", which can then be loaded and executed
using IREE's runtime.
—>Receives isolated mathematical processing kernels wrapped inside structural
hal.executable blocks. and translates them into raw machine binaries via compiler
backends like LLVM (for CPUs like ARM, RISC-V, x86) or SPIR-V (for GPUs).
—> These instructions act as the "orchestrator," detailing when to allocate buffers, manage
resource ownership, and issue execution commands to the hardware.
—> other path can be followed , can convert actions directly to the LLVM dialect to emit platform-specific
host executables or WASM modules or translate into native c source code.
This phase takes the input dialects (like Linalg and Arith) and partitions the
massive tensor graph into distinct data-parallel execution chunks called dispatch
regions.
This layer handles the timeline of execution, inserting dependency information and
optimizing transient memory allocation boundaries.
This is the final unified layer. HAL dialect isolates these two representations.
It produces an IR representation consisting of two distinct parts:
—> Command Buffers: A serialized sequence of host-side VM control commands
that dictate the order, memory allocation, and scheduling of the execution
—> Device Executables: The raw, tiled mathematical workloads (the actual
kernel computations) wrapped inside the dispatch regions.
At this point, the compiler splits the single stream into Host Code Generation
and Device Code Generation simultaneously.
—> Receives scheduling commands and memory allocation definitions parsed by the HAL dialect.
—> lowered into a compact, specialized bytecode format designed to be interpreted by the
lightweight IREE runtime VM.
Host Code generation
—> LLVM Backend (CPUs): Translates nested matrix and vector loops into
LLVM IR to compile tailored machine code for architectures like ARM, RISC-V, or
—> SPIR-V Backend (GPUs): Bypasses LLVM entirely to target standard GPU
execution engines like Vulkan, WebGPU, or OpenCL.
—> Accelerator Targets: Utilizes specialized LLVM dialects to directly produce
PTX (NVIDIA CUDA) or ROCDL (AMD HIP) GPU hardware configurations.
—>VMVX Safe Fallback: Compiles math kernels into platform-agnostic Virtual
Machine Vector Extensions if native instruction set compilers are missing.
Device Code Generation
IREE MODULES(VM Bytecode)
—> Packages the generated host logic and device workloads into a single,
cohesive .vmfb (Virtual Machine FlatBuffer) file
—> The host orchestration path and the device math path are entirely
decoupled from one another.
—> Host Component (The Controller): it is an intermediate bytecode designed to be interpreted by a highly efficient runtime engine.
This bytecode strictly constitutes:
. Memory Allocations: Commands detailing exactly when and where to grab chunks of memory for active inputs, weights, and temporary variables.
. Asynchronous Semaphores: Synchronization gates that dictate how the Host and Device should stay in sync without locking up processing cores.
. Execution Timelines: A scheduled list of commands that record operations into hardware command buffers.
. Dispatch Sequences: Instructions that tell the system exactly when to hand specific computational tasks over to the hardware.
—> C Source Code Form (.c): Generates pure, readable C code via the EmitC
path. This maps the host scheduling logic straight to native runtime API calls,
allowing you to completely remove the bytecode interpreter and save 15–30 kB
of space on bare-metal systems.
—> Static Library Form (.o / .a): Compiles the device math kernels into fixed
machine-object binaries. These are statically linked ("welded") directly into the
main application software at compile-time, eliminating all runtime library discovery
and symbol-lookup overhead.
—> Shared Dynamic Library Form (.so / .dll): Bundles the mathematical compute
kernels into a dynamic shared object. IREE builds an ultra-lightweight dynamic
linker directly into its runtime so the system can hot-swap or update models on
the fly without altering the main host firmware.
—> Device Component (The Workload): Embeds the pre-compiled hardware-
accelerated computation kernels (such as NVIDIA PTX/SASS or SPIR-V binaries)
directly inside the file's binary data payload.
—> Execution: At runtime, an ultra-lightweight virtual machine interpreter reads the
host bytecode to manage data flow and streams the embedded math kernels straight to the hardware driver.
—> An IREE Module is not a single isolated file type; it is a unified
deployment package created by combining one Host option (the orchestrator)
and one Device option (the math kernels).
—> The Standard .vmfb Path: By default, the compiler merges the Host's VM
Bytecode and the Device's Shared Library into a single, self-contained Virtual
Machine FlatBuffer (.vmfb) binary file for zero-copy runtime execution.
—> The Embedded Bare-Metal Path: For tiny, memory-constrained hardware, the
compiler outputs a combination of Host C Source (.c) via EmitC and a Device
Static Library (.o). This lets you compile the entire model directly into your
system firmware, completely removing the bytecode interpreter to save 15–30 kB
of space.
—> Separation of Concerns: This decoupled design ensures that regardless of
the deployment format chosen, the Host layer always handles high-level graph
synchronization and scheduling while the Device layer maps directly to target
hardware acceleration (like ARM, RISC-V, x86, or NVIDIA PTX).
The IREE runtime acts as the thin execution engine that loads, links, and runs the
compiled module packages on actual hardware. It is split into two foundational
sub-layers designed to mimic the split structure of the compiler:
—> The Virtual Machine (VM): A lightweight, register-based interpreter execution engine
that processes the Host Control logic (VM Bytecode or direct C APIs) to handle orchestration,
allocations, and control loops.
—> The Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL): An extensible device driver framework that provides a
unified API for managing memory types, recording command queues, and executing the compiled Device
Dispatch Workloads across diverse compute backends (like CPU, Vulkan, or CUDA).
IREE Runtime
IREE Runtime VM
Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL)
The IREE runtime Virtual Machine (VM) is a lightweight, register-based execution
engine written in isolated, standard C. Its primary job is to process the Host
orchestration logic with minimal memory overhead and zero dynamic allocations during
hot execution paths.
Bytecode Interpretation Loop
The interpretation loop is the engine room of the Virtual Machine. Every time your
application runs a model, the VM enters a continuous loop that executes three strict
phases for every instruction: Fetch, Decode, and Dispatch.
-> The Opcode Fetch: The VM maintains an instruction pointer pointing directly
to the memory-mapped .vmfb byte stream. It reads the first byte—the opcode (the
command identifier, such as a branch, object creation, or a call out to the hardware
abstraction layer)—and then increments the pointer.
->Computed Goto / Switch Dispatch: To achieve maximum performance in C, the VM uses
compiler-specific features like computed gotos (using label arrays in GCC/Clang) or highly optimized
switch statements. This jumps the instruction pointer directly to the C function handling that specific
opcode, minimizing branch mispredictions.
-> Direct HAL Bridge: When the VM encounters an instruction to execute a model workload,
it doesn't do the math itself. It decodes the instruction arguments and hands them directly
over to the Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) API to queue up the work on the physical
processor or GPU.
—> Registered Based Architecture: A register-based model allows complex operations to be expressed in
fewer, more expressive instructions.No pushing/poping as we can directly refer to registers.This drastically
reduces the total instruction count in the bytecode stream, resulting in a smaller .vmfb file footprint and fewer
interpretation cycles.
—> The VM enforces a stable, hardware-agnostic ABI boundary. It decouples the core model control logic
from the underlying hardware, allowing the same bytecode file to run globally across any device, while
supporting seamless bidirectional execution calls between compiled bytecode and native system C code.
—> The VM manages its heavy resources using high-performance,
deterministic reference counting. Hidden runtime memory allocations are
completely eliminated; the compiler pre-allocates and tracks buffer lifecycles
upfront, making execution entirely predictable and safe for constrained systems.
The Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) is IREE's universal device driver
framework. It acts as a standardized translation layer between the agnostic
Virtual Machine (VM) and the physical hardware.
Purpose:
The HAL provides a single, unified C API for managing hardware memory
and executing parallel work. Because of the HAL, the host program (the VM) can
control completely different backends—like an NVIDIA GPU, an Apple GPU, or a
local CPU thread pool—using the exact same set of execution commands.
2. The Driver Ecosystem
The HAL sits directly on top of small, pluggable drivers. When the VM invokes a
generic HAL function, the HAL routes that call to the registered driver for your
specific hardware backend:
CUDA Driver: Translates the HAL commands into raw NVIDIA driver
calls (e.g., cuMemAlloc, cuLaunchKernel).
Vulkan Driver: Translates the commands into GPU graphics/compute queue
operations (VkCommandBuffer).
Local-Task Driver: Routes the math operations to an internal CPU thread
pool designed for parallel processing.
The HAL acts as a single, standardized interface wrapper that hides the
differences between various hardware processors—translating generic calls
for memory buffers and execution commands into vendor-specific language
(like CUDA, Vulkan, or CPU threads).
1. A Unified API Interface:
3. Non-Blocking Execution (Timeline Semaphores)
it eliminates runtime CPU stalls by using 64-bit Timeline Semaphores to handle
dependencies. The host CPU submits entire chains of command buffers to the
hardware queue and moves on immediately, leaving the physical device driver to
track and unblock the mathematical execution phases at bare-metal speeds.
